lines.text: Spatial relations describe how objects are positioned relative to one another, and English expresses these relationships with remarkable precision. Horizontal relations use terms like 'adjacent' (immediately next to), 'adjoining' (sharing a boundary), 'parallel' (running side by side at equal distance), and 'perpendicular' (meeting at a right angle). Vertical relations include 'overhead' (directly above), 'elevated' (raised higher), 'sunken' (lowered below the surrounding level), and 'level with' (at the same height). Containment and enclosure use 'within' (inside the boundaries of), 'enclosed by' (completely surrounded), 'surrounded by' (encircled), and 'embedded in' (fixed firmly within). Proximity ranges from 'immediate' (right next to) through 'nearby' and 'in the vicinity' to 'remote' and 'distant'. Alignment describes how things line up: 'centred', 'offset', 'flush with' (perfectly aligned on the same plane), and 'staggered' (arranged in an alternating pattern). Overlap and intersection use 'overlapping' (partially covering), 'intersecting' (crossing each other), and 'converging' (meeting at a point). These terms appear constantly in architecture, design, urban planning, interior decorating, and technical writing. Mastering spatial vocabulary allows learners to describe environments precisely, follow technical instructions accurately, and communicate about physical arrangements with the clarity that advanced English demands.

lines.text: British garden design uses precise spatial language: 'borders' (edges), 'beds' (planting areas), 'paths winding through', 'pergola over', 'trellis along'. The concept of 'rooms' within a garden — distinct spaces separated by hedges — is quintessentially English.
